newsitem.title: USA: Fran not seen bringing much rain to U.S. Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Fran not seen bringing much rain to U.S. Midwest.

text.p: Remnants of Hurricane Fran were expected to bring only light rains to western Ohio and very little precipitation to Indiana, meteorologists said.

"As the tropical remnants of Fran push to the north through Sunday, eastern Ohio and Pennsylvania will see some shower activity develop, though it will not be widespread the further west one travels," said Smith Barney's Basilio Lopez.

Western Ohio could receive 0.10 to 0.75 inch of rain with 60 percent coverage while extreme eastern portions of Indiana should see 0.10 to 0.50 inch with 20 percent coverage, said Weather Express Chief Forecaster Fred Gesser.
"As you go into northwest Indiana and Illinois, there's no effect of Fran other than maybe some clouds," Gesser said.

Weather Services Corp's Joel Burgio said the Appalachian Mountains would keep most of the rain east of the corn belt. He said the mountains serve as a "sponge," soaking up much of the moisture and keeping it out of the Midwest.
Temperatures were expected to peak in the 80s (degrees Farenheit) Friday and Saturday, but a cooler pattern was seen moving into the western corn belt late Saturday, Burgio said.
Low temperatures should be in the 50s F across most of the region early next week with some 40s F possible in Minnesota.

"The cooler air early next week will slow development some, but it is not a frost threat in any way," Lopez said. "With the coolest conditions expected in the east, the crops there will definitely be under the gun through the middle of the month."
Scattered to widely scattered showers were possible with the cooler front, Lopez said.
"Rainfall will range from 0.40 to 1.50 inches, with the concentration of the precipitation falling in the northwest sections of the belt," he said. "Coverage will be around 50 percent biased north."
The front should lose most of its moisture as it moves east early next week, forecasters agreed. Coverage estimates dropped to about 30 percent for Indiana, they said.
